sec.title: Changing Global Epidemiology of Inflammatory Bowel Diseases: Sustaining Health Care Delivery Into the 21st Century
Ashwin N. Ananthakrishnan,*,a Gilaad G. Kaplan,‡,§,a and Siew C. Ngk,a
sec.p: *Division of Gastroenterology, Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts; ‡Department of Medicine, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada; §Department of Community Health Sciences, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada; and ||Department of Medicine and Therapeutics, Institute of Digestive Disease, State Key Laboratory of Digestive Diseases, LKS Institute of Health Science, Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, China

Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis have emerged as global diseases. They affect over 2 million individuals in the North America, 3.2 million in Europe, and millions more worldwide. The recent decades have been characterized by several important changes in the epidemiology of these diseases, in particularly an increasing incidence rates in newly industri- alized countries experiencing a westernization of lifestyle. While rates of surgery have experienced a temporal decline attributable in part to increasing availability of medical treatments,earlierinitiationofeffectivetherapy,andchanges in clinical practice, the healthcare costs associatedwith these diseases have continued to increase, in part due to costly therapies. Robust epidemiologic and experimental studies have defined the role of the external environment and microbiome on disease pathogenesis and have offered op- portunities for disease prevention by modifying such factors. We propose several important steps that are necessary to provide globally sustainable inflammatory bowel disease care in the 21st century.
Keywords: Inflammatory Bowel Disease; Crohn’s Disease; Ul- cerative Colitis.

I n the 21st century, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has emerged as a global disease. Hundreds of population-based studies on the incidence and prevalence of IBD have been reported throughout the world.1,2 The compilation of these studies paints a striking pattern for the epidemiology of IBD with broad implications from improving the understanding of the pathogenesis of IBD to highlighting the evolving burden of disease. These epide- miologic patterns are best conceptualized through separate lenses focused on the Western world, newly industrialized countries, and the developing world.3 As the economic sta- tus of a country improves, fundamental changes occur within a society: urbanization, industrialization, changing agricultural practices, evolving health care infrastructure, sanitization, and adoption of a Western lifestyle. In this milieu, IBD emerges and flourishes within society.3
The changing patterns in the epidemiology of IBD will impact the future burden of IBD. In Western countries prevalence is rising and the IBD population is aging.4

sec.title: Hospitalizations and surgeries are declining, whereas
sec.p: the cost of therapeutics are climbing. Incidence is climbing in newly industrialized countries in Asia and Latin America, and with time may approximate the burden of IBD in the Western world.2 Addressing the global rise of IBD requires a tandem effort of modulating in environmental risk factors to prevent IBD and inno- vating delivery of health care to patients with IBD.5 The purpose of this review is to highlight trends in epide- miologic patterns of IBD, explore modifiable environ- mental exposures that may reduce incidence of IBD, and discuss the evolving global health care burden of IBD.

sec.title: Changing Patterns in the Epidemiology of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
sec.p: During the 20th century, IBD was considered a disease of the Western world. The prevailing theory was that IBD occurred because of shared genetic susceptibility inter- acting with environmental exposures of the Western lifestyle.3 In the Western world, the incidence of IBD took off post–World War II. A systematic review identified hundreds of population-based studies that indicated that most countries reported steadily rising incidence of IBD throughout the Western world.1 Rochester, Minnesota,6 and Cardiff, United Kingdom7 conducted longitudinal epidemiologic studies dating back to the mid-20th cen- tury: decades of data highlighted a steadily rising inci- dence of IBD in these well-defined regions. The rising incidence of IBD in the 20th century alluded to environ- mental determinates ingrained in Western society as be- ing the predominant drivers of IBD development.5
At the turn of the 21st century, epidemiologic studies from the Western world indicated a paradigm shift in the aAuthors contributed equally to the article.

Countries from the Western world started reporting stabilization of incidence and even decreasing incidence in some regions.2 Although spo- radic elevations in IBD incidence are still being reported, the overall incidence is coalescing around a range be- tween 5 and 15 per 100,000 person years for both Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC).2 More- over, the ceiling in the incidence of IBD seems to be between 40 and 50 per 100,000 person-years.2 Future studies are needed to confirm if the peak in the incidence of IBD has been reached in the Western world. During the 20th century, the incidence of IBD was sparsely reported in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, and the data available showed dramatically lower values compared with the Western world.1 Studies on the migration of individuals from the developing world to the Western world indicated that migration increased the risk of developing IBD particularly in the first- generation offspring of immigrants.8,9 At the turn of the 21st century, numerous higher quality epidemiologic studies from newly industrialized countries in Asia and Latin America reported sharply rising incidence of IBD.10,11 For example, incidence of CD and UC increased by 11.1% and 14.9%, respectively, per year in Brazil from 1988 to 2012,12 and 4.0% and 4.8% per year in Taiwan from 1998 to 2008.13 In contrast to the Western world, a peak in the incidence of IBD in Asia and Latin America has yet to be reached. Future studies are needed to determine whether the rising incidence of IBD in newly industrialized countries will eventually reach the same peak of incidence observed in the Western world. Although awareness, access to health care, and advancinginfrastructurecontributestotherisingincidence of IBD in newly industrialized countries, the primary driving force is environmental exposure associated with the Westernization of society.3 Prevailing theories suggest that environmental exposures, particularly those early in life, alter the diversity, composition, and function of the intestinal microbiome leading to IBD development later in life. Modulating environmental exposures in the general population, and particularly in patients at greatest sus- ceptibility for IBD, has the potential to prevent the devel- opment of IBD and reduce its incidence in the future.3

sec.title: Clinical Lessons From Observational Studies of Environmental Risk Factors
sec.p: Environmental factors play a major role in IBD, including, but not limited to: antibiotic use, childbirth mode, breastfeeding, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs use, air pollution, diet, and urban environ- ments.14-16 The timing of environmental exposures var- ies across the age spectrum of IBD with some factors specific to early life (eg, breastfeeding) and others more relevant for adults diagnosed with IBD.17

Cigarette smoking is one of the most consistent risk factors for IBD. In UC, quitting smoking increases the risk of developing UC in the Western world. Similarly, in Asia, the odds of being diagnosed with UC was 2-fold higher among individuals who quit smoking.15 However, unlike consistent reporting of Western cohorts, whereby smoking is a risk factor for CD development and worsens disease outcomes,18 data from the Asia-Pacific Crohn’s and Colitis Epidemiologic Study Group (ACCESS) study showed that smoking was not a risk factor for CD in Asia.15 Furthermore, there are specific examples from Western studies whereby the association between CD and smoking has not been shown in particular pop- ulations (eg, Israeli Jews, seniors) and regions of high smoking prevalence do not correlate with regions of high IBD prevalence.19 Hence, smoking is a predictor of aggressive disease course but is unlikely to account for worldwide trends in disease incidence. Several studies have suggested a significant associa- tion between childhood antibiotic exposure and the onset of IBD later in life. However, discrepancies of this association across different populations and ethnicities are observed. For example, greater use of antibiotics in childhood increases the risk of developing UC in the Western world, but data from Asia seem to contradict this notion because children exposed to antibiotics were protected from developing UC.15 Furthermore, antibiotic use reduced the risk of CD in Middle Eastern migrants to Australia but increased the risk in white persons.20 Risk factors likely differ at different stages of industrializa- tion; hygiene factors might be important in developing countries, whereas immunologic factors may play a more important role in developed countries. A meta-analysis of 17 papers examined the association between breast- feeding and IBD and demonstrated a strong inverse as- sociation with both CD and UC.21 Likewise, the ACCESS inception cohort study found that infants living in Asia who were breastfed for more than 12 months were 7 times less likely to develop UC. A New Zealand study found that breastfeeding for a longer duration lowered the odds of developing IBD.22 Overall, breastfeeding has a marked protective effect on development of CD and UC and a beneficial dose effect of breastfeeding has been observed. Prevention studies have focused on general pop- ulations, using serum repositories to identify changes in individuals who are known to develop disease later, and on at-risk populations, such as family members. In the PREDICT (PRoteomic Evaluation and Discovery in an IBD Cohort of Tri-service Subjects) study, prediagnostic sera from soldiers with IBD was collected and analyzed for antimicrobial antibodies and protein markers; immune dysregulation was detectable in serum up to 6 years before the diagnosis of CD.23 The proportion of positive antimicrobial markers including ASCA IgG, ASCA IgA, anti-OmpC, anti-Fla2, anti-FlaX, and anti-CBir1 were found to progressively increase toward disease diag- nosis.23,24 Importantly, individuals with higher serum levels of antimicrobial antibodies and a different profile of proteins years before diagnosis were at highest risk of

May 2020 Global IBD in the 21st Century 1253 presenting with a complicated disease phenotype including fistula/abscess or strictures. There was also an inverse relationship between the time to first complica- tion and the magnitude of serology markers.25,26 These findings suggest that innate immune activation with involvement of complement pathways may occur early in the natural history of complicated disease; this highlights the potential role of serologic markers as a noninvasive tool to screen and detect preclinical IBD and to identify individuals at higher risk of progression to complications. Studying preclinical IBD in the general population is challenging because of the enormous sample size and long duration of follow-up necessary for disease to develop. Given that the strongest established risk factor for the development of IBD is having a first-degree relative (FDR) with the disease, earlier cross-sectional studies focusing on healthy relatives of patients with IBD reported altered intestinal permeability, positive antimicrobial marker, raised fecal calprotectin, and altered stool bacterial composition in a subset of IBD relatives. However, the significance of these biomarkers and their predictive value for disease development re- mains unclear.27 The Genetics, Environmental, Microbial (GEM) Project is a multicenter study that recruits FDRs age 6–35 years of affected CD probands, and prospec- tively collects biologic samples (blood, urine, stool), and environmental exposure data assessing etiologic factors in CD. It was found that elevated fecal calprotectin was significantly associated with a future diagnosis of CD in asymptomatic FDRs of patients with CD.28

Emerging evidence has shown that early life, including neonatal life, is a critical window for development of gut microbiome and certain environmental exposures to ne- onates could impact the risk of different diseases later in life.29 In IBD, this concept has been supported by epide- miologic data demonstrating an increasing incidence in individuals who spent years living in an urban environ- ment during childhood who received antibiotics during early life or who had not been breastfed.30 A recent population-based Swedish study showed that children exposed to antibiotics had a 93% increased risk of developing very early onset IBD and CD and that risk was driven by exposures occurring during the third trimester of pregnancy compared with earlier trimesters.31 In addition, a Canadian population-based cohort showed that maternal diagnosis of IBD was the strongest risk factor for the offspring developing IBD and risk factors included infection in the first year of life, suggesting that the most important predictor for subsequent diagnosis of IBD is a genetic effect and a close mother-child relation- ship. What remains less clear is whether infections themselves are the risk factor for subsequent IBD or whether it is instead the exposure to antibiotics to treat the infections that incur the most risk.32

The importance of early life exposures in the risk of developing IBD suggests that the composition, diversity, and function of the intestinal microbiome is related to the development of IBD.33 Prospective studies, such as the MECONIUM study (Exploring MEChanisms Of disease traNsmission In Utero through the Microbiome), which follows pregnant women with IBD and their infants by collecting biosamples, clinical, and dietary data to study their microbiome, biomarkers of disease susceptibility, and environmental exposures, will help to better un- derstand the very early risk factors (as far back as during pregnancy) for disease development and help develop preventive strategies during this early life period. Mothers with IBD had altered bacterial composition and diversity in their gut during pregnancy with enrichment of Gammaproteobacteria and depletion of Bacter- oidetes.34 Furthermore, infants born to mothers with IBD showed lower diversity and altered bacterial gut composition in up to at least 3 months of life. The altered microbiota induced changes to the adaptive immune system in germ-free mice, suggesting that microbial factors in maternal IBD may impact the immune system of offspring. Overall, targeting perturbations of the microbiome in pregnant women with IBD or neonates could foster the development of a healthy microbiome in the offspring, and it is also possible that primary in- terventions at this stage could be established to reduce the risk of diseases later in life.35,36

Epidemiologic evidence suggests a link between di- etary Westernization and CD. Specific mixtures of mac- ronutrients and emulsifiers within the diet have been shown to affect intestinal permeability, gut microbiota density, and predisposition to intestinal inflammation in IBD in animal studies.37-40 Human studies, such as the ENIGMA41 study, aim to investigate the role of food ad- ditives and diet in subjects with CD across different populations and geography (China, Hong Kong, Australia). There is increasing interest in diet as a treatment of CD, especially exclusion diets, specific car- bohydrate diet, and IBD anti-inflammatory diet.42,43

There are several ongoing diet prevention studies. The ADDapt trial (ADDitives using and app trial)44 is a randomized controlled trial in patients with stable CD that investigate the efficacy and acceptability of a low- emulsifier diet by using a mobile telephone application and dietary counseling. Crohn’s Disease Treatment with Eating (CD-TREAT)45 is a pilot open-label clinical trial to evaluate an individualized diet similar in nutritional composition to exclusive enteral nutrition in patients with active CD. Although more data are still needed from well-designed randomized controlled trials and to elucidate which aspects of the diets are having an effect, diet is likely to be important in altering the course of IBD. Several exclusion diets are showing promise, yet until more data emerge it is prudent to focus on the most consistent recommendations and not to compromise nutritional intake. To conduct successful intervention studies, the trigger of IBD needs to be established and existing bio- markers or predictive tools should have high predictive value to justify potential adverse effects from screening,

We need better understanding which therapies or interventions can ameliorate or reverse the immunologic changes in the preclinical phase of IBD and which therapies and preventive measures high-risk in- dividuals will be willing to accept when faced with a probability of developing the disease. Importantly, the duration of which a preventive therapy or strategy is to be continued to prevent or halt disease progression needs to be defined. A potential research program would include smoking cessation programs in FDRs of patients with IBD, multiplex families, or asymptomatic individuals with positive serology or microbial markers. Other strategies include the avoidance of antibiotics in children or pregnant mothers with IBD in the absence of a strong indication or potentially manipulate their diet to elimi- nate food that contains food additives. However, it will be challenging to prove the benefit of such interventions in controlled trials given the need for a large group size and a long interval between the targeted intervention and actual clinical benefit to be detected. In the absence of high-quality interventional studies, evidence-based recommendation of environmental risk factor modifications thatprevent the future development of IBD is lacking. However, while awaiting these data, clini- cians can still offer advice to their patients. Box 1 highlights a checklist for prevention of modifiable environmental risk factors: breastfeed, avoid smoking, optimize vitamin D, judicious use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antibiotics, nutritious diet, regular physical activity, regular sleep patterns, minimize stress, and maintain a healthy weight.30 Each of these factors contribute only modestly to the attributable risk of IBD, but collectively they represent an approach toward prevention of IBD. Moreover, all of these factors are associated with overall healthy living. Reducing the incidence of IBD is critical in stemming the rising burden of IBD to society.

sec.title: Predictions for the Future: Compounding Prevalence, Morbidity, and Health Care Costs
sec.p: In the mid-part of the 20th century, countries in the Western world had increasing incidence with low prev- alence of IBD.5 IBD has been historically a disease of the young, and with no cure and relatively low mortality, the rising incidence accelerates the prevalence over time.46

For example, the prevalence of CD and UC in Olmsted County, Minnesota in 1965 was 28 and 117 per 100,000,47 climbing to 133 and 229 per 100,000 by 1991,48,49 respectively. Prevalence continues to climb at the turn of the 21st century despite the stabilization of incidence. As long as the number of new diagnoses of IBD outpaces mortality, prevalence will continue to rise, an epidemiologic concept referred to as compounding prevalence (Figure 1).5

The compounding prevalence of IBD was highlighted in a national Canadian study of 7 provinces. Despite the declining incidence rates of IBD observed in most prov- inces, the prevalence continued to rise in Canada because of the longevity of Canadians with IBD. Consequently, models forecast that prevalence of IBD will increase by 3% per year leading to a rise in prevalence from 0.7% in 2018 to 1% by 2030.4 Compounding prevalence of IBD is likely occurring in countries throughout the Western world. A recent study from Lothian, Scotland replicated the Canadian models: in 2018, the prevalence of IBD in Scotland was 0.78%, and was forecasted to reach 1.02% by 2028.50

Compounding prevalence of IBD in the Western world has significant future implications. As the number of patients with IBD grows, health care providers and health care systems will be challenged to provide affordable and high-quality care.5 The future burden of IBD is not limited to the number of patients with IBD but also encompasses the changing demographics of IBD. In the Western world, patients with long-standing IBD are aging every decade such that seniors with IBD represent the fastest growing demographic with IBD.51 An aging IBD population enhances the complexity of care because physicians must navigate IBD care against comorbidities of advanced aging.52

In contrast, the prevalence today remains low in newly industrialized countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. However, analogous to the Western world in the 1970s, these regions have rising incidence that will eventually drive prevalence. Whether epidemiologic patterns of newly industrialized countries will mimic those of the Western world, just shifted forward in time, is unknown. But, if compounding prevalence occurs in countries outside of the Western world, the number of people with IBD throughout the world will spike to tens of millions of people. Consequently, the IBD community needs to coalesce around understanding how the burden of IBD will evolve over time and focus on research that

May 2020 Global IBD in the 21st Century 1255 prevents disease development. Addressing the burden of IBD is a 2-prong strategy involving innovations in the delivery of care to regions experiencing compounding prevalence while instituting environmental interventions that meaningfully reduce the incidence of IBD.5

In parallel with increasing incidence and compound- ing prevalence, studies have also demonstrated secular trends in IBD-related morbidity and changes in rates of hospitalization, surgery, and health care costs. Globally, paralleling to the patterns of incidence, there is a varia- tion in the hospitalization and surgery burden in IBD. An analysis that pooled data from 34 member countries for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Devel- opment found significant global variation in hospitaliza- tion rates for IBD.53 Higher hospitalization rates were observed in North America (33.9 per 100,000 in United States) and Europe than in Asia and Latin America. However, although countries with the highest hospitali- zation burden exhibited declining rates over time, those countries where IBD incidence and hospitalization were rare demonstrated the greatest annual increases.53

However, even within high-prevalence regions, there continues to be an increase in IBD-related hospitaliza- tions in some countries. For example, between 1990 and 2003, hospitalization rates for a primary diagnosis of IBD in the United States increased from 9.3 to 17.1 (per 100,000 population) in CD and 8.2 to 12.4 per 100,000 in UC.54 In contrast, population-based studies of IBD co- horts in Canada, which has a similar disease prevalence, demonstrated a decline in age-adjusted hospitalization and surgical rates for CD.55,56 Thus, data on temporal trends in IBD-related hospitalizations are mixed overall and difficult to interpret given subjectivity in reasons for hospitalization and length of stay, and the potential role of non-IBD-related comorbidities. In contrast, rate of surgery has consistently decreased over the past 3 decades in many57 but not all58 studies. Using the United Kingdom primary care database, Burr et al59 examined temporal trends in the rate of surgery from 1994 to 2003. From a cohort of 3059 incident cases of CD, they determined that 26% underwent resection by 10 years after diagnosis, and 20% of those with 1 resection required a second resection within 10 years. However, there was a significant reduction in both the rate of first resection (reducing from 44% to 21% at 10 years of disease) between 1994 and 2003, and a similar reduction in second resections from 40% to 17%.59

Similarly, a Canadian population-based study demon- strated that between 2002 and 2010, there was a 3.5% annual decrease in rate of surgery.60 There was a greater decline in emergent (-10.1% per year) compared with elective surgeries (þ3.7% per year). A comprehensive systematic review identified cumulative resection rates at 1, 5, and 10 years after diagnosis to be 16%, 33%, and 47% in CD and 5%, 12%, and 16% in UC. However, over the past 6 decades, there was a significant decrease in the rate of surgery at each of these time points in both diseases.57,61

The improvement in surgical rates has not been observed across all spectrum of disease severity. In hospitalized severe UC, the short-term rates of colectomy have stabilized at around 25%–30% without the corre- sponding decline in colectomy observed in large population-based cohorts that included patients of all spectrum of disease severity.62 Furthermore, the extent to which such temporal decreases in rate of surgery can be attributed directly to availability and efficacy of biology therapy, particularly anti–tumor necrosis factor agents, and the fraction attributable to changes in med- ical practice and threshold for surgery remains to be clearly established. A health administrative database study from Ontario province in Canada examined the impact of infliximab introduction on IBD-related hospi- talization and intestinal resections in patients with CD and UC during the period between 1995 and 2012. Despite an increase in use of biologic medications during

1256 Ananthakrishnan et al Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology Vol. 18, No. 6 the study period, a decrease in UC- or CD-related hos- pitalizations and surgery could not be attributed to the availability of infliximab.63

The young age of onset of CD and UC, their pro- tracted life-long course interspersed with periods of active disease requiring hospitalization and surgery, results in substantial economic costs as a consequence, both in direct health care costs and indirectly from productivity losses. There has been an increase in overall health care costs in patients with IBD in most cohorts, with the rate of increase outpacing that in patients without IBD.64

An initial estimate of the cost attributable to CD and UC in the United States was provided by Hay and Hay65 who estimated an annual average cost of CD and UC to be $6561 and $1488, respectively. This could be extrapo- lated to total direct costs in the United States of $1–1.2 billion for CD and $0.4–0.6 billion in UC. Using data from 1994–1995, Feagan et al66 estimated an annual cost of care for CD to be higher at $12,417. Updating the direct costs in 2004, Kappelman et al67 extrapolated health care costs associated with IBD in the United States using commercial insurance claims data. Based on a calculated annual cost of $8265 and $5066, respectively, for CD and UC, they estimated total IBD-associated direct costs in the United States to be $3.6 billion for CD and $2.7 billion for UC, which was nearly 3-fold higher than the estimate 1 decade ago. These estimates in the United States are broadly similar to that observed in other countries, although numerically higher than reported from Europe.68

Consistent across all studies of health care costs are that costs have shifted from being driven by hospitali- zation and surgery in the estimates from the mid-1990s to primarily being determined by pharmaceutical costs, in particular biologics. Earlier studies suggest that hos- pitalizations accounted for 55% of health care costs in UC, significantly higher than recent estimates of 31%.65,67 In comparison, outpatient pharmaceutical costs have increased from 4% in the study by Hay and Hay65 to 36% in the commercial insurance claims study by Kappelman et al67 in data separated by 1 decade (Figure 2). An elegant population-based study from the Korean National Health Insurance Claim database, covering nearly the entire South Korean population, showed that there has been a significant increase in the per capital cost between 2006 and 2015.69 The strongest determinant of overall costs was an increase in phar- maceutical costs, primarily that of anti–tumor necrosis factor therapy.69 A similar study in the Netherlands recruited patients with CD or UC, receiving care from 15 hospitals, to complete a web-based questionnaire regarding their direct and indirect health care costs.70

Overall, although CD was associated with greater health care costs than UC, the use of anti–tumor necrosis factor biologic therapies was the main driver of costs in both diseases, accounting for 64% and 31% of health care costs in CD and UC, respectively.

sec.title: Moving Toward Sustainable Global Inflammatory Bowel Disease Care
sec.p: IBD is a global disease. Although the incidence and prevalence remains highest in the industrialized coun- tries of the Western hemisphere, the size of populations of countries where the disease is emerging suggests that the greatest number of affected patients will be residing in the latter regions.3,11,71 Although the tremendous ad- vances in therapeutics has improved the ability to ach- ieve remission in high-incidence countries, lifelong biologic therapy from diagnosis in all patients is economically unsustainable even in these countries let alone the emerging economies with competing soci- etal priorities. To achieve sustainable global IBD care, we propose several important steps (Box 2). First, as described previously, health care costs have evolved from primarily being driven by surgeries and hospitalizations to that associated with pharmacologic treatment, biologics in particular. In addition, the need for parenteral administration and risk of infections with systemic immunosuppression challenges the logistics of administration and safety of these therapies in emerging incidence countries. Thus, there is a need to optimize the cost of these agents and develop oral and targeted drugs that may be more sustainably delivered and safer. The cost disparity in IBD care is further amplified by an effective treat-to-target strategy where monitoring tools are often expensive when required repeatedly. Thus, easier tools to monitor disease activity and assess response to treatment are needed. Second, there is often a delay of up to 2–4 years before diagnosis of IBD. Such a delay is associated with increased risk of complications.72 This delay may be further exaggerated in low-incidence countries where competing diagnoses, such as tuberculosis, are more common. This can contribute to disease refractoriness and irreversible damage. Thus, there is an important need to optimize diagnostic strategies and develop tools that allow for early recognition of disease before signif- icant irreversible complications. Research has consistently shown that up-front effec- tive treatment early on in the course of disease is more effective than an incremental step-up treatment approach.73 Such strategies may be particularly impor- tant in emerging countries where lifelong biologic treatment may not be sustainable, whereas an early, short-term, and aggressive treatment (to modify long- term course of disease and reduce need for long-term therapy) may be the cost-effective approach. The existing IBD treatment algorithm relies on sequential treatment of patients with successive thera- peutic classes on failure of the initial therapy. This results in treating patients, often for extended periods of time, with expensive yet ineffective therapies. As one thinks of providing sustainable global IBD care, the ability to more precisely match patient and therapy is essential to avoid unnecessary drugs and provide more cost-effective care. Health care costs after a patient has developed CD or UC are high. However, if inexpensive and effective primary (or secondary) prevention strategies are devel- oped that could identify and intervene at the level of, or even before, preclinical disease, then the morbidity and costs associated may be prevented.
